narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 69% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly outweighed other information.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5 worked in the opposite direction. It is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the much stronger negative influence of your class rankings.

Your low family income, 27.5 LSAT score, and full-time study plans also played supporting roles, but the model gave them less weight than your year-by-year class standing.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and LSAT score before reapplying. Stronger grades and a higher test result would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. Consider targeted tutoring, practice exams, or a post-baccalaureate program to demonstrate upward momentum. Many applicants succeed on a second attempt after making these improvements.
